excerpts: Dear brothers and sisters, good morning!
Thank you to everyone!
The Cathedral of Paris, which just seven years ago seemed mortally wounded by a devastating fire, has now been rebuilt and is more splendid than ever.
That disaster sparked a positive reaction at every level, some more visible and practical, others more hidden and of a spiritual nature.
Its restoration was a test of the possible collaboration between the Church, the State, public institutions and civil society.
Two completely different locations, yet two complementary events, almost united spiritually.
At Notre-Dame there were priests and deacons, consecrated persons, and pastoral workers; at the stadium there was the new French generation.
Young people who sang and shouted, but who also remained silent, listening.
Attentive and emotional faces, which revealed hearts yearning for truth and love.

There, the sign of rebirth appeared in a surprising way: the liturgical assembly, which in the vast Square brought together the priests, the choir and a remarkable crowd, extended all the way along the Avenue des Champs Élysées up to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.
And Europe was reborn, founded on those principles of democracy, solidarity and fraternity amongst peoples, which owe much to its Christian roots.
Dear friends, the theme of my pastoral Visit to France was “Pour que le mode ait la vie”, “That the world may have life”.
They are Jesus’ words, which encapsulate His entire mission of salvation and which, during the Journey, fully expressed the Gospel meaning of every encounter.
I extend my heartfelt plea to all parties to choose the path of dialogue.
Armed conflict never solves problems but only worsens them, leaving in its wake a trail of death, destruction, and resentment.
Only honest engagement can lay the foundations for lasting peace.
It is my fervent hope that the international community will offer its generous and timely contribution, to ensuring that all humanitarian aid be provided to those in need.

excerpts: Some of you have crossed continents, traveled far, and brought your joys and burdens to this sacred grotto.
May this pilgrimage rekindle the flame of faith in your homes and parishes.
Take the consolation of Lourdes back to your neighbors, your loved ones and the whole French people.
The prophet Ezekiel reminds us, “When a righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he shall die for it.”
Indeed, now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation.
God wants us to live, to open our eyes and return to him.
Jesus himself is quite direct in calling us to repentance.
As Saint Luke tells us, “Unless you repent, you will all perish”.
This promise, made right here, has a particular force in this land of France, and it challenges the way we think today.
In the face of current trends that seek to redefine the value of human life in illness, suffering and old age, the grotto of Massabielle stands as a place of Christian hope.
We must therefore use our freedom to say yes to Christ, relying on his grace, like Mary.
Penance!
She repeats the word three times.
And she asks Bernadette to perform certain acts of penance.
Are we slow to understand?
This call to conversion also concerns the Church herself as she makes her earthly journey.
In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within her, we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze.
Recognizing our own faults is essential to our spiritual growth.
Pilgrims, brothers and sisters, you will not leave Lourdes as you arrived.
The Virgin Mary heals our outlook and changes our hearts, giving them peace.
In your countries, dioceses and families, become living witnesses to this divine strength and tenderness, which help us to persevere towards our goal.
Sustained by the prayers of the sick and the love of our Mother, walk with confidence into the future.
Amen.

excerpts: Dear brothers and sisters,
I give thanks to God for the grace of being here with you today, in the Place de la Concorde, to celebrate the Eucharist.
It is truly good and pleasant when brothers and sisters dwell together in unity to proclaim God’s greatness.
“If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink”.
This is the cry of a humble and passionate heart whose deepest, most existential thirst continues to grow.
Jesus responds to our profound desire for relationship, for communion with God, in whom the fullness of life forever resides.
In the first reading, the prophet Ezekiel saw water flowing out from the Temple and spreading through the desert, purifying and bringing life to everything it touched.
When we think that our work is finished at last and our efforts have been rewarded, that inner emptiness often returns, deeper than before.
Are we content with material goods, immediate satisfactions, the countless little idols that promise us everything but leave our hearts empty?
He carries the weary and wounded sheep on his shoulders, and gently brings back those who have gone astray.
Jesus reveals God’s unconditional love for us.
In his eyes, none of us is merely a number or an entry in a register, but a unique and irreplaceable person.
You long to rediscover a horizon filled with light and to build a renewed nation upon roots nourished by faith.
You are called to bring hope wherever discouragement and spiritual dryness prevail.
From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.
I think of you, dear families, who, despite the many difficulties you face each day, persevere courageously in your vocation and mission.
May the tangible presence of Jesus within you never run dry.
Through her free and trusting “yes”, she became the humble vessel, chosen by God, in which the Father’s love took flesh and gave itself to the world.
Amen.

excerpts: Mr Director-General,
Mr Chairperson of the Executive Board,
Your Excellencies,
Ladies and Gentlemen,
1, par.
Since 1952, the Holy See’s Permanent Observer Mission has examined and accompanied UNESCO’s initiatives from this standpoint, offering its specific contribution to the dialogue among nations.
Speaking to this assembly, my venerable predecessor Saint John Paul II observed that “genus humanum arte et ratione vivit.”
In the field of education, the Catholic Church is heir to an ancient tradition.
For centuries, her communities have founded schools and universities, taught people to read and write, and have been present even in the poorest and most remote places.
With the Global Compact on Education, my predecessor Pope Francis sought to make this experience part of a broader educational covenant, open to the contribution of all.
Indeed, every generation is called to grapple with this question, especially in the face of tragedies that, regrettably, occur even today.
It is precisely those in need who suffer the greatest consequences of this forgetfulness, whenever their humanity is betrayed or cast aside, exploited or deceived.
By that labor, we may cultivate the earth or disfigure it, create works of art or destroy them.

Humanity had come to realize that scientific progress, when severed from wisdom, can turn into a weapon of destruction; that culture, when subjected to ideology, can degenerate into falsehood and propaganda; and that education, when it abandons the truth, can become an instrument for manipulating consciences.
Peace cannot be built by treaties alone, nor by compromises between opposing forces.
Eighty years later, the words of your founding Charter have lost none of their force.
Yet we also see how profoundly this common principle is threatened by forms of barbarity that fuel rivalry and conflict.

The paradox has become increasingly evident: while “intelligence” is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognize the inalienable dignity of human persons, whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and, when deemed no longer productive, are rejected and discarded.

For the Christian faith, the mystery of the human person finds its fullest light in Christ, who, “in the very revelation of the mystery of the Father and of his love, fully reveals humanity to itself and brings to light its very high calling” (SECOND VATICAN ECUMENICAL COUNCIL, Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes, 22).
Where there is harmony, different voices find agreement, and the nations you represent are thus brought together in concord.
In this regard, I would like to appeal to two images from the Bible, the great cultural treasury of humanity.
The tower of Babel represents a unity imposed through domination.
The outcome of this pride, exalted and then brought low, is dispersion.
The presumption of making oneself like God and subjecting peoples to a single yoke leads to a confusion of languages and a failure to understand one another.

Today, the temptation of Babel reappears in a globalization pursued without fraternity, in rapacious forms of neocolonialism, in ideological impositions and in all those “contacts without bonds” that reduce human life to commerce.
Science itself, when reduced to a technique of power, no longer serves to elevate the human person, but instead risks degrading the fruits of human endeavor.

Today, in particular, we possess the means to connect people and continents instantaneously, yet, at the same time, we are witnessing new forms of isolation, material and spiritual poverty, and abandonment.

Without a shared ethical foundation, the many channels of communication risk multiplying false information and giving currency to words devoid of meaning, thereby hindering dialogue rather than fostering it.
Artificial intelligence amplifies this problem.
Yet human beings cannot live without meaning.

That is why education in this area is essential, and I welcome UNESCO’s initiative through its Media and Information Literacy (MIL) program, which promotes the responsible use of media and digital tools.
In the digital age, their vulnerability must never become an opportunity for exploitation.
The corruption of culture which we are considering finds its redemption in the public square of Pentecost.
Communion in no way suppresses diversity.
In the proclamation of peace, the richness of cultures becomes a bearer of a universal truth.
Those who teach and those who conduct research know that error enslaves us to ignorance and superstition.
The human being cannot be understood by separating what belongs together: body and soul, personal life and relationships, our relationship with others and with the environment.

The touchstone by which we can assess our commitment is the care we show for the littlest and for the poor: children in their mothers’ wombs andin the various theaters of war, persons with physical and intellectual disabilities, the elderly, migrants refugees, and all those arrogantly excluded as unproductive.
They are the true test of our claims to respect human dignity, and their protection and promotion extend also to creation.
Opposed to this is a will to exploit and plunder, extracting as much as possible from every living being, consuming without safeguarding, destroying without cultivating.
Where social peace prevails, peoples flourish in justice.
Amid the many complex and pressing issues of the present time, our world regards international institutions with mixed feelings.
In this case, we see the urgent need to promote a virtue that seems as greatly desired as it is rarely found, namely the virtue of trust.
Every child born into this world brings new hope.
As we cooperate in this work, religious traditions have a culturally necessary and irreplaceable role to play.
Religions voice our questions regarding the origin of life and its purpose.
We are not journeying toward oblivion.
Indeed, it is the younger generations who observe our actions most closely.
Thank you.

excerpts: Mr President,
Distinguished Authorities and Members of the Diplomatic Corps,
Ladies and Gentlemen,
Together, they make up a people whose diverse origins have enlivened and enriched the nation and its democracy.
My visit to France begins in Paris, the country’s capital, often known as the City of Light.
With its cathedral schools, universities and academies dedicated to the pursuit of truth, France has helped to shape the outlook of peoples far beyond its borders.
French expertise is synonymous with excellence in numerous fields.
I express my deep appreciation to the many artists, builders, technicians and skilled workers who took part in the restoration.
It showed that something considered irreparably destroyed can be reborn through mutual cooperation, and it bore eloquent witness to the unity born of commitment to a common cause.
May this remarkable achievement encourage all those responsible for the country’s political, social and religious life to work tirelessly and as one, inspired by a firm and lively hope.
France is a land with deep Christian roots.

From the time of Saint Irenaeus and the baptism of Clovis, the soul of the nation has drawn from Christianity a rich spiritual, cultural, intellectual, artistic and missionary élan that continues to be felt in our world today.
So it was that humanism flourished in sixteenth century France, as a means of uniting the heritage of classical Greece and Rome with the Christian faith.

Liberty, equality and fraternity are not simply words emblazoned on the front of your public buildings; they refer to universal ethical imperatives that also find in the Gospel message an inexhaustible source of inspiration and fulfillment.

The question of respect for human dignity and the fundamental rights and freedoms that derive from human nature is one that arises in every age and must necessarily keep pace with societal change and technological progress.
To be sure, “over the centuries, technological development has significantly improved the living conditions of humanity.

In his own day, Georges Bernanos saw the threat that blind obedience and irresponsibility could lead to a “Paradise of Machines,” and pointed out that French civilization had instead sought for centuries to form free men and women who are fully responsible for their actions.
This often brings the risk of self-delusion.

I am concerned at times by those trends in society that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death.
Indeed, authentic secularity does not exclude religion but is capable of valuing it as an educational resource.
Their service will be more efficient and beneficial to all if both institutions develop better cooperation” (SECOND VATICAN ECUMENICAL COUNCIL, Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes, 76).
Education is especially critical in this regard and is one of the principal areas of cooperation, finding concrete and fruitful expression, in particular, through the Fonds pour les écoles d’Orient.
The stockpiles of armaments built up in various countries must be reduced all round and simultaneously by the parties concerned.
Nuclear weapons must be banned.
A general agreement must be reached on a suitable disarmament program, with an effective system of mutual control” (Encyclical Letter Pacem in Terris, 112).
In the face of rumors of war and the varied crises troubling our world, France is called to remain a tireless champion of peace and multilateralism, particularly within our beloved Europe.
May your liberty grow in constant concern for the common good.
May your fraternity embrace the entire human family.
I entrust these hopes to the maternal intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the principal patroness of France.
